Family comparison can help too — if close relatives who live apart and have different lifestyles still share the same cravings or metabolic issues, that leans toward genetics. Vitamin D comes from two main sources: your skin makes it under UVB light, and you get some from diet (like fortified milk, fatty fish, or even certain mushrooms). Sometimes, your body’s ability to process and store vitamin D improves if other factors change — like better overall nutrition, improved gut absorption, or less inflammation. On top of that, even subtle changes in your daily habits you might not notice (walking outside a bit more often, eating different foods, taking supplements without realizing some have vitamin D) can tip the scale.

Also, vitamin D takes weeks to months to reflect lifestyle changes, so the reason your recent test looks better could be due to stuff you did months back — even if it wasn’t intentional. And there’s natural seasonal variability, meaning if you got tested during the sunnier part of the year, you might have naturally higher levels without changing much.

In short: your bones are no longer ‘sad’ because your body either sneakily got more D into the system or made better use of what it had. No membership to the Church of Sunbathing required.
